text.text: Data report 80 pairs of jeans 20 brands men's & women's

Front and back pocket measurements of men's and women's jeans from popular brands. Across the 80 pairs in this file, men's front pockets average 23.13 in maximum height against 14.33 for women's — a ratio of 1.61 . Back pockets, pocket widths and prices sit close to parity. The gap is deep, front-only, and it does not shrink as the price goes up.

Source: data/measurements.csv — 80 rows × 16 columns, no missing values. Every number on this page is computed from that file in the browser; the pandas expression behind each headline figure is listed in the appendix .

mean price, men's vs women's — , not in pocket

Each row is one pair of jeans: a brand, a product name, a fit label, a fabric string, a price, and nine pocket measurements — maximum and minimum height and width for the front pocket and the back pocket, plus the height of the front rivet.
80 jeans · 40 men's, 40 women's · exactly two of each per brand
schematic only — the file does not say where each measurement starts and ends

Every one of the 20 brands contributes two men's jeans and two women's jeans, so the comparisons below are never driven by an uneven sample. Fit labels differ by side: women's jeans are labelled skinny (20), straight (16) or boot-cut (4); men's are labelled skinny (12), straight (12), slim (8), boot-cut (7) or regular (1).
schematic — the file does not define the measurement points

Front pockets carry six numbers ( maxHeightFront , minHeightFront , rivetHeightFront , maxWidthFront , minWidthFront ), back pockets four ( maxHeightBack , minHeightBack , maxWidthBack , minWidthBack ).
Counts of jeans by fit label and side, as recorded in the style and menWomen columns.

The file records no units. Garment specs of this kind are normally centimetres, and the numbers behave like centimetres (a 23 × 16 front pocket on men's jeans, a 14 × 15 one on women's), so this page reads them as cm — but every figure quoted is exactly the value in the file.
All 1,280 cells of the table are filled. The only cleaning needed is cosmetic: the brand column holds 22 raw spellings that reduce to 20 brands once case and whitespace are normalised.
Every one of the 80 jeans, plotted by the maximum height of its front pocket. The two lanes barely touch: the shallowest men's pocket in the file (20.0) is deeper than 39 of the 40 women's jeans.
Maximum front pocket height, all 80 jeans
each dot is one pair of jeans · dashed line = group mean · hover for the product
Men's heights run 20.0–28.0 (mean 23.13, sd 2.06); women's run 11.5–21.5 (mean 14.33, sd 2.10). The spread inside each group is almost identical — the whole difference is a shift.
maximum height × maximum width, as a rough proxy for pocket room
Multiplying the two front-pocket numbers gives 378.41 for the average men's jean against 217.97 for the average women's — a ratio of 1.74.
On the front height — the shallowest point of the opening — women's jeans fall below 15, against men's.
Mean of each recorded measurement, men's (blue) against women's (rust).
Where the gap is — and where it isn't
Divide each men's mean by the matching women's mean and the pattern is unmistakable: the gap is a front-pocket, vertical phenomenon. Widths are near parity, and back pockets are near parity.
Men's mean ÷ women's mean, for each measurement
means of the four back-pocket numbers
Maximum front pocket height is the outlier at 1.61. Maximum front width is 1.08, maximum back height 1.06, maximum back width 1.03.

Women's back pockets are only slightly smaller — 15.12 vs 16.01 in maximum height. The front rivet, by contrast, sits higher on men's jeans on average, 7.06 vs 6.25 , and the men's rivet range is wider (4.5–9.2 against 4.5–7.5).
Read together: the visible, decorative back pocket is treated much the same on both sides of the gender split. The pocket you actually put things in is not.

The gap is not one brand's habit — it is the industry's. Fifteen of the 20 brands give men's jeans a mean front pocket height at least 1.5× the women's. Levi's is widest at 2.09; Abercrombie is narrowest at 1.13.
Mean maximum front pocket height per brand
sorted by the men's-to-women's ratio · each brand = two men's jeans and two women's jeans

Levi's (25.75 vs 12.35, ratio 2.09), Guess (24.00 vs 12.00, 2.00) and Wrangler (27.75 vs 14.50, 1.91) sit at the top; Abercrombie (22.25 vs 19.75, 1.13), American Eagle (21.50 vs 17.50, 1.23) and H&M (20.75 vs 16.75, 1.24) at the bottom. Brand spellings are normalised, so Guess and 7 for All Mankind appear once each.

Mean price is effectively identical — $81.18 for men's jeans, $80.32 for women's. Within each side, the correlation between price and front pocket height is slightly negative : -0.262 for men's, -0.151 for women's.
x = price, y = maxHeightFront × maxWidthFront · dashed lines = group means

The two clouds sit at the same prices but different heights. The cheapest jeans in the file — H&M's women's Skinny Ankle High Waist at $9.99 — carry a maximum front pocket height of 19.0 , tied for second-deepest among the women's jeans. The most expensive — True Religion's women's Slim Straight at $249.0 — measures 14.5 .
Price per unit of front pocket area
price ÷ (maximum front height × maximum front width)
mean, median and range by side

The means line up almost exactly. The medians go the other way — women's jeans in this sample are more expensive in the middle of the range (78.75 vs 69.72), while the men's median is pulled down by budget workwear brands.
women's jeans cost about 1.8× as much per unit of front pocket
Women's jeans cost 0.386 per unit of front pocket area on average (median 0.341); men's cost 0.219 (median 0.185). Same shelf price, less pocket.
Both extremes of the price range belong to women's jeans, and neither extreme is a deep pocket: the $9.99 H&M pair measures 19.0, the $249.0 True Religion pair 14.5.
The fit label tells you nothing
If pockets followed the fit label, a boot-cut or straight jean would carry more room than a skinny one. They don't. Within each side the style means are almost flat, and the two sides never meet.
Mean maximum front pocket height by style label
bar length = mean; n = number of jeans with that label
six women's jeans labelled straight have "boot" in the product name

All six are women's jeans; on the men's side, every product with "boot" in its name is labelled boot-cut . Fit labels in this file are best read as marketing categories, not measurements — which is why every comparison on this page uses the measured numbers instead.

Women's means: boot-cut 14.25 (n=4), skinny 14.27 (n=20), straight 14.42 (n=16) — a spread of 0.17. Men's means run from 21.50 (the single "regular" jean) to 23.90 for the 8 slim jeans. Gender explains the height; the label does not.
The two sides are also built differently. Women's jeans lean on stretch fibre; every rigid, 100%-cotton jean in the file is men's.
percentage parsed out of the fabric string · each dot is one pair of jeans
9 of the 80 jeans carry cutout = TRUE
Cutout jeans cost far more on average — 133.10 against 74.11 — and they are mostly men's (6 of the 9). They come from four brands only: True Religion (4), Guess (2), J. Crew (2) and Uniqlo (1).
cotton share of the fabric string
Men's jeans average 93.3% cotton (range 53.0–100.0), women's 80.8% (range 30.0–99.0). All eight 100%-cotton jeans in the sample are men's: 8 on the men's side, 0 on the women's.
The file does not define what "cutout" means, so this page treats it as a flag rather than a feature. It is the one column that separates strongly on price.
Four things a reader should know before quoting these numbers.

Brand spellings are inconsistent. The brand column holds 22 distinct raw strings that reduce to 20 brands once case and surrounding whitespace are normalised — "Guess " with a trailing space, and "7 for all Mankind" beside "7 for All Mankind". Everything here uses the normalised form.

"min" is not always smaller than "max". In 14 rows the recorded minHeightFront is larger than maxHeightFront — 12 of them women's jeans, 2 men's. The two columns are therefore not the two ends of one measurement, and this report quotes them separately rather than averaging or differencing them.
Fit labels drift from product names. Six women's jeans labelled "straight" have "boot" in the name, including Levi's Classic Bootcut .

No units, one size, one sample. The file states no unit, records no waist size, and gives one measurement per product rather than a range across sizes — so nothing here speaks to how pockets scale with size, and nothing measures a pocket after wear.
The full file, sortable and filterable. Shaded cells mark the deeper pockets; hover any row for its fabric string.
Columns are the file's own, in order. Fabric is abbreviated to its cotton share; the full string appears on hover. Area is computed on this page as maxHeightFront × maxWidthFront.
Appendix: every number, and the code behind it

Each finding below was computed from data/measurements.csv with the pandas expression shown, loaded as measurements = pd.read_csv("data/measurements.csv") with pd and np in scope. Run any of them to reproduce the figure exactly.
The table holds 80 jeans described by 16 columns of brand, style, fabric, price and pocket measurements.
Each half of the sample spans 20 brands once spellings are normalised for case and whitespace: 20 distinct brands among the men's jeans and 20 among the women's.
The design is balanced: for every brand the number of men's jeans and the number of women's jeans both have a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 2.

Men's jeans average a maximum front pocket height of 23.13 and a minimum front height of 18.08, against 14.33 and 13.23 for women's; front widths are much closer, 16.37 vs 15.18 at the maximum and 13.36 vs 12.26 at the minimum.
The average men's front pocket is 1.61 times as tall as the average women's front pocket, 61.44% taller.

The gap lives in front pocket height and almost nowhere else: the men's-to-women's ratio of means is 1.61 for maximum front height, 1.08 for maximum front width, 1.06 for maximum back height and 1.03 for maximum back width.

measurements.groupby('menWomen')[['maxHeightFront', 'maxWidthFront', 'maxHeightBack', 'maxWidthBack']].mean().pipe(lambda g: pd.Series({c: g.loc['men', c] / g.loc['women', c] for c in g.columns})).round(2)
Taking maximum height times maximum width as a rough pocket area, men's front pockets average 378.41 and women's 217.97, a ratio of 1.74.

measurements.assign(front_area=measurements.maxHeightFront * measurements.maxWidthFront).groupby('menWomen').front_area.mean().pipe(lambda s: pd.Series({'men': s['men'], 'women': s['women'], 'ratio': s['men'] / s['women']})).round(2)
Maximum front pocket height runs from 20.0 to 28.0 in men's jeans (mean 23.13, standard deviation 2.06) and from 11.5 to 21.5 in women's jeans (mean 14.33, standard deviation 2.10).
The smallest maximum front pocket height among the men's jeans is 20.0, and 39 of the 40 women's jeans fall below it.
On the minimum front pocket height, 34 of the 40 women's jeans are below 15, against 5 of the 40 men's jeans.

Mean price is nearly the same on both sides of the gap, 81.18 for men's jeans and 80.32 for women's, while the medians go the other way, 69.72 for men's and 78.75 for women's; prices span 39.99 to 209.0 for men's jeans and 9.99 to 249.0 for women's.
Paying more does not buy a taller front pocket: within each group the correlation between price and maximum front pocket height is -0.262 for men's jeans and -0.151 for women's.
The cheapest jeans in the sample, H&M's women's Skinny Ankle High Waist at 9.99, record a maximum front pocket height of 19.0 and a minimum front height of 13.5.
The most expensive pair in the sample, True Religion's women's Slim Straight at 249.0, has a maximum front pocket height of 14.5.
Per unit of front pocket area, price divided by maximum front height times maximum front width, women's jeans cost more: mean 0.386 and median 0.341, against mean 0.219 and median 0.185 for men's.
Style labels say almost nothing about women's pocket size: mean maximum front pocket height is 14.25 for the 4 boot-cut jeans, 14.27 for the 20 skinny jeans and 14.42 for the 16 straight jeans.

Men's style labels are similarly flat: mean maximum front pocket height is 23.57 for the 7 boot-cut jeans, 21.50 for the 1 regular jean, 22.71 for the 12 skinny, 23.90 for the 8 slim and 22.92 for the 12 straight.

Ranked by the men's-to-women's ratio of mean maximum front pocket height, Levi's is widest at 2.09 (25.75 vs 12.35), then Guess at 2.00 (24.00 vs 12.00) and Wrangler at 1.91 (27.75 vs 14.50); Abercrombie is narrowest at 1.13 (22.25 vs 19.75).

measurements.assign(b=measurements.brand.str.strip().str.lower()).pivot_table(index='b', columns='menWomen', values='maxHeightFront', aggfunc='mean').assign(ratio=lambda x: x['men'] / x['women']).round(2).sort_values('ratio')
15 brands give their men's jeans a mean maximum front pocket height at least 1.5 times that of their women's jeans.

measurements.assign(b=measurements.brand.str.strip().str.lower()).pivot_table(index='b', columns='menWomen', values='maxHeightFront', aggfunc='mean').assign(ratio=lambda x: x['men'] / x['women']).query('ratio >= 1.5').shape[0]
There are no missing values in the file: the total number of NaN cells across the whole table is 0.

Back pockets are close to parity: men's jeans average 16.01 maximum height and 13.70 maximum width against 15.12 and 13.34 for women's, with minimums of 13.47 vs 12.58 for height and 12.16 vs 11.74 for width.
The front rivet sits higher on men's jeans on average, 7.06 against 6.25, and the men's range is wider, 4.5 to 9.2 versus 4.5 to 7.5.
Cotton percentages parsed from the fabric strings average 93.3 for men's jeans (range 53.0 to 100.0) and 80.8 for women's jeans (range 30.0 to 99.0).
Every 100% cotton jean in the sample is men's: 8 among the men's jeans and 0 among the women's.
Nine jeans carry the cutout flag and they are the expensive ones: their mean price is 133.10 against 74.11 for the 71 without it.
Among the jeans flagged with a cutout, 6 are men's and 3 are women's; among those not flagged, 34 are men's and 37 are women's.
The brand column holds 22 distinct raw spellings that reduce to 20 brands once case and surrounding whitespace are normalised.
In 14 rows the recorded minimum front height is larger than the recorded maximum front height, 12 of them women's jeans and 2 men's.

pd.Series({'rows': int((measurements.minHeightFront > measurements.maxHeightFront).sum()), 'women': int(((measurements.minHeightFront > measurements.maxHeightFront) & (measurements.menWomen == 'women')).sum()), 'men': int(((measurements.minHeightFront > measurements.maxHeightFront) & (measurements.menWomen == 'men')).sum())})

Six women's jeans are labelled style 'straight' although their product names contain 'boot': Arizona Perfect Boot, Lucky Sweet Boot, Levi's Classic Bootcut, 7 for All Mankind Bootcut, Guess Tailored Mini Boot and Express Barely Boot Midrise.
— a report on : front and back pocket measurements of men's and women's jeans from 20 popular brands, 80 pairs in total.

Built as a single offline HTML file. No external libraries, fonts or network calls: the data is embedded, the charts are hand-drawn SVG, and the statistics are recomputed in the browser from those rows.
